auxiliary_material: Detailed mechanistic pathways for specific metabolites (SCFAs, inosine, formate, tryptophan derivatives) and their receptors (AhR, GPR41/43, TCR ligands) which provide context for why quantification matters.
Summary of ongoing clinical trials (Table 2) combining microbiome interventions with ICI, which may serve as potential sources for finding primary metabolite quantification data if queried further.
Recommendations for contamination-aware workflows (RIDE checklist, Nature Microbiology 2025 consensus) relevant to ensuring the validity of any intratumoral metabolite data found.
Discussion of anatomical routes (portal-venous, lymphatic, systemic) that affect metabolite distribution, informing the interpretation of plasma vs. tumor concentration differences.
outline_action: Use this review to justify the methodological gap in the literature planning section and to cite the emerging technologies (imaging MS, biosensors) as the state-of-the-art solution. Search the references cited in this review (e.g., those regarding TMAO in TNBC or formate in murine models) to retrieve the primary study reports for specific methodological details. Prioritize finding primary studies that explicitly compare intratumoral concentrations with matched fecal/plasma samples in ICI-treated human cohorts, as this review indicates such data is sparse.
remaining_gap: The supplied text is a review and does not provide the primary methodological details (e.g., specific mass spectrometry parameters, sample processing protocols, patient cohort sizes) of the studies it references that performed intratumoral quantification. It confirms the gap exists and names the technologies but does not list the specific primary studies or their direct comparative data (tumor vs. fecal/plasma) in full detail.
useful_material: The review explicitly confirms the methodological gap, stating that for most metabolites and delivery formats, validated models linking input to in-tissue exposure are lacking, and cancer-immunology use of biosensing/imaging tools is nascent.

It identifies specific techniques capable of direct quantification, including imaging mass spectrometry, spatial multi-omics, and functional biosensors, noting they enable co-registration of metabolite exposure with immune-cell states in human tumors.

It cites examples of intratumoral metabolite quantification in specific contexts, such as higher intra-tumoral/plasma TMAO associating with activated immune microenvironment in triple-negative breast cancer patients responding to immunotherapy.

It distinguishes between quantification in fecal/plasma samples (common) versus intratumoral samples (rare/challenging), highlighting the low-biomass and contamination risks associated with tumor tissue analysis.
